meta.title: Projects. Launch and Grow — course 4 · AIVIS.ONE
s01.t03: In this course you will learn to
s01.t04: launch a small project by a strict order of work (a protocol): a constitution (your main project document, two pages), a stage plan (a sprint page), a task with a criterion — a clear check
s01.t05: work step by step and call an independent review — by someone other than the author
s01.t06: release the result (show the finished thing to people) safely, able to go back, and not work “on a hunch”
s02.t02: Agent projects fall apart without written records: the documents are in charge, not the chat
s02.t05: A decision left in a chat does not exist for the next chat. The agent (a chat with a role and a task that carries out steps itself) forgets, takes on too much and writes “done” without checking.
s02.t08: is written in documents, not in chat history
s02.t10: names its limits and how to check it before work starts
s02.t12: needs a shown result and the look of someone who did not do it
s02.t15: Is a strict order needed? A one-off task belongs in a plain chat, as in course 1. Several documents, stages, a return in a week: a strict order.
s03.t02: The same roles as in course 3: you decide, three work
s03.t07: Decides: the goal, the choices between options, the yes before a release
s03.t08: writes only the constitution, the main document
s03.t10: Leads, sets the assignment, accepts the result
s03.t14: the only one who changes them
s03.t18: One chat per role, as in course 3. A worker does not make the choice: it returns the question to you.
s04.t07: A goal for weeks, with its own plan and clear signs of success
s04.t08: a working sign-up form for the book exchange
s04.t10: A finished part of a stage, with its own result
s04.t11: the form with checks; the “my sign-ups” list; the release
s04.t13: One small change with its own check
s04.t14: the form refuses an empty name
s04.t15: Three levels are enough to start.
s05.t02: The project remembers a document, not a chat
s05.t03: The stage plan (one page): the goal, how we will know it worked, “what we do not do”, the parts it is made of.
s05.t04: The next action: one concrete action, never “carry on”. A new chat starts from it.
s05.t05: The “stop” rule: a check failed twice, something outside the task is needed, rules disagree, something is published or deleted: the agent stops and asks you.
s05.t06: The “for the human” section: what you decide and what to open first.
s05.t07: At the end, the stage plan in our example said so itself: “Status: closed”; the stage results are in a separate document, then the owner’s decision.
s06.t02: Five short documents before the first stage
s06.t03: The idea: what the project is, for whom, what success looks like. One page at most.
s06.t04: What it is made of: its parts, and what we leave out on purpose.
s06.t05: The roadmap: stages as a list, one line a goal. It is not a to-do list; in course 3 the matching file was the “Plan”.
s06.t06: What the work needs: which computer you have, which programs are needed, where the project files are kept.
s06.t07: The to-do list: kept apart, everything not yet in work.
s06.t08: Password check: no passwords or access keys to your services may sit in the project documents.
s07.t02: The Project protocol skill: add it and take the first step
s07.t03: Leads you step by step and gives short templates: a small project
s07.t04: It restates first: the skill (a ready-made instruction for a chat) retells your project in its own words and waits for your yes. If a strict order is not needed, it says so.
s07.t05: One step at a time: from the starting documents to the release; it shows only the template for your step and names the next at the end.
s07.t06: Roles as in course 3: one chat per role, you decide.
s07.t07: Your first step: add the skill and write the starting documents with it.
s08.t05: What we build and for whom
s08.t06: Who sees what and the visitor’s main path
s08.t07: What a person enters and how their data is protected
s08.t11: Detailed tasks: those are written separately
s08.t12: In the example, the owner’s answers became two pages: a three-field form, two possible exchange dates and the rule “a visitor sees only their own sign-ups”. The shared tablet at the door is this example’s setting, not advice to you. This is a real run, but the course author answered and checked in the owner’s place.
s09.t02: Plan the whole stage first, then do the work
s09.t03: Goal in one sentence: a working sign-up page on this computer — the form, the list, the release.
s09.t04: Success criteria: each a check that either passes or fails, or a visible fact. For example, an automatic check (a program that runs all the checks itself) with no failures.
s09.t05: “What we do not do”: accounts, e-mail, payments, a server of our own (a separate computer for the site), other people’s ready-made pieces of programs.
s09.t06: Parts before the work starts: the form and its checks; the “my sign-ups” list; the release.
s09.t07: The owner confirms the stage plan before any work starts.
s10.t02: A task: what may change, what may not, how we check, the level of risk
s10.t05: No limits, no check: the agent decides what “decent” means and says “done” itself.
s10.t08: the form refuses an empty name and shows a clear message
s10.t10: the page, the file with the form rules and a new file of checks
s10.t12: the documents, other people’s ready-made pieces of programs, the book and date rules
s10.t14: the name check runs and passes (the agent runs it; you type nothing)
s10.t17: A criterion is a check that either passes or fails. Someone other than the writer runs it.
s11.t02: Scout, a check that fails first (red test), do, verify the result, close
s11.t03: Scout: a worker only reads and reports facts. In the example: the project held only documents, no form and no program.
s11.t04: A check that fails first: it must fail while the thing it checks does not exist yet. That is how we know it checks anything at all.
s11.t05: Do: the smallest change that makes the check pass. The orchestrator does the work.
s11.t06: Verify: run the checks and look at the numbers (how many passed, how many did not), not “seems to work”.
s11.t07: Close: the report; the next step and the decisions go to the navigator.
s12.t02: The higher the risk, the earlier the stop
s12.t08: this run had no such task
s12.t10: Do it, verify, show the numbers
s12.t11: the empty name: a new feature, but nothing is saved yet
s12.t13: Show the plan and wait for the owner’s yes
s12.t14: the “my sign-ups” list: privacy is the core promise
s12.t15: At high risk: scout, a report with the plan, stop until the yes, and only then the check that fails first, and the work.
s13.t02: A check is insurance, and a check that fails first is proof
s13.t03: Insurance: a check guards against the system doing the wrong thing with a person’s data.
s13.t04: An edge case is a rare situation: an empty name, a name of spaces only, a date outside the two possible ones.
s13.t05: From the run: first we tested the checks themselves: while an empty stand-in that accepted anything sat in place of the program, 2 of the 3 checks failed, as they should. Then the real program was written and all 3 passed. The worker did not count the very first failure: the check failed not on an error but because it could not find a file.
s14.t02: Automatic protection beats a polite request: a rule asks, protection blocks
s14.t03: Before starting: before work the agent must read the named documents. Not read, no work.
s14.t04: The “stop” rule: the agent halts and shows the result before the next step.
s14.t06: A check that fails first: it fails before the program exists.
s14.t07: One stage, one chat: start from a clean sheet and the documents, not a long chat history.
s14.t08: Start with the cheapest: ask to see the result of the check. “It all passes” with no result shown is not proof. The protection is set up in an assistant on your computer (course 3, slide 12); in a plain chat your own habit stands in for it.
s15.t02: One writes, another checks — by six questions
s15.t05: In the example all of the worker’s checks passed, but two checks from the task were not among them. “Passed” is worth what was checked.
s15.t14: what was decided is written the same
s15.t16: every place the edit touches is checked
s15.t18: what was removed is gone everywhere
s15.t19: Findings are labelled: SERIOUS (BREAK) stops the work, MISSED (GAP) does not, MINOR (NIT) is cosmetic (the same three labels as in course 2).
s16.t02: What stops the work, what is put off
s16.t07: The list was not cleared between visitors
s16.t08: returned; the fix is a separate task
s16.t10: No check covered it: all 16 passed
s16.t11: first add the missing checks; on the earlier version (with the error) 4 of them failed, so they do catch the error
s16.t13: Damaged records are silently overwritten; no name length limit
s16.t14: put off; the owner picks the length
s16.t16: A stale word “planned” in a document
s16.t18: How it really went: the course author planted this error on purpose. The worker’s report said two checks were not done, but did not name the error. The reviewer did not read that report and found the other visitors’ sign-ups in the list, and the checks that missed them, on their own. The shared tablet is the example’s setting, not advice.
s17.t02: Nine habits instead of working by feel
s17.t03: Before: do not write by feel · read what already exists first · a check that fails first.
s17.t04: During: small checkable steps · do not trust your own result: let someone else check it · do not copy a rule into several documents, they will drift apart.
s17.t05: After: know your requirements: have a written list of what should result · fix now, do not put it off in secret · know exactly what you changed.
s17.t06: A habit weakens when you are tired; automatic protection does not: it blocks the same on any day.
s18.t02: Four traps and what to hand to an ordinary program, not to AI
s18.t07: The model (the program that writes the chat’s answers) hurries: skips checks and edge cases
s18.t08: ask for checks outright, name the edge cases in the task
s18.t10: It gets built around as if it were a foundation
s18.t11: mark it “temporary” and write it into the put-off list
s18.t13: The model grabs one meaning and misreads the rest
s18.t14: use an exact word or invent your own
s18.t17: a new chat with the documents loaded
s18.t18: Exact work to a program, meaning to the model. A program answers “where” and “how many”, the model “why” and “what for”. In the example an ordinary program (one that follows fixed rules exactly the same every time, like a calculator) checks the name, not a request to “check carefully”.
s19.t02: A decision card: question, options, choice, why
s19.t03: Question: one line on what is being decided.
s19.t04: Options: three, each argued. If it feels like yes or no, find a third: defer or combine.
s19.t06: Why: a reason that can be checked. Cards are kept one after another in one document.
s19.t07: From the run: the worker handed in the work and all its checks passed. Accept it? Options: accept; send back as it is; send back and ask for a check on what was missed, one that fails first. The third was chosen: “passed” is worth only what was checked.
s20.t08: 31 of 31 checks passed at the close
s20.t09: Bad input is refused with a message
s20.t12: The list shows this visit only
s20.t13: met in the program; on screen the course author looked, not the owner
s20.t14: the checks added with the fix
s20.t15: No ready-made pieces of programs from other people
s20.t17: an automatic search of the project’s files found nothing
s20.t18: The owner signs up on a phone in under a minute
s20.t20: the course author checked in the owner’s place
s20.t21: The stage closed with one criterion not met: the course author answered and checked in the owner’s place, so the real check moved to the next stage.
s21.t02: Check first, then replace the old version with the new — and keep a way back
s21.t07: You put ready files there and they are shown as they are
s21.t08: the site does not need to store visitors’ data
s21.t10: A separate computer for the site: you set it up and look after it
s21.t11: you need full control of the data
s21.t13: The service runs and maintains it for you
s21.t14: the site must cope with many visitors without you fussing over equipment
s21.t15: The rule: the new version’s checks pass — you replace the old with the new, the old one stays beside it, going back takes one action.
s21.t16: In the example the release was only on the course author’s computer: the working version was replaced by the new one, and the previous one could be restored with one action. Nothing was published online.
s22.t09: From a task to a finished skill (course 2).
s22.t18: A project by a strict order, step by step (course 4).
